lesson.title: How Many Versions to Test: Levels of a Factor
lesson.summary: The levels of a factor are the specific values or categories a factor is set to during an experiment, and the total number of treatments in a multi-factor experiment equals the product of the number of levels of every factor.
lesson.body:
The levels of a factor are the specific values, amounts, or categories that the factor is set to during an experiment. If fertilizer amount is a factor, its levels might be none, 5 pounds, and 10 pounds per plot. If drug dosage is a factor, its levels might be 0 milligrams, 50 milligrams, and 100 milligrams. Levels turn an abstract factor into something a researcher can actually apply to an experimental unit.

When an experiment includes multiple factors, the total number of distinct treatments equals the product of the number of levels of each factor, since every treatment is one specific combination of levels, one from each factor. In the fertilizer and watering example from the previous section, fertilizer amount had 2 levels and watering frequency had 2 levels, giving 2 times 2 equals 4 total treatments. If a third factor were added, say sunlight exposure with 3 levels, shade, partial sun, and full sun, the total number of treatments would jump to 2 times 2 times 3 equals 12 distinct treatments, one for every combination of a fertilizer level, a watering level, and a sunlight level.

This multiplication has real consequences for how many experimental units a study needs. If researchers want at least 6 plots per treatment combination in the 12 treatment version of the fertilizer, watering, and sunlight experiment, they need at least 12 times 6 equals 72 plots in total. Adding factors or adding levels within a factor can quickly make an experiment expensive to run, which is why researchers often carefully limit the levels of a factor to only the values that are scientifically interesting, rather than testing every value imaginable.

Levels can be quantitative, such as 5 pounds versus 10 pounds of fertilizer, or categorical, such as brand X fertilizer versus brand Y fertilizer versus no fertilizer. Quantitative levels let researchers ask whether the response changes gradually as the level increases, for example whether yield keeps climbing as fertilizer amount increases from 5 to 10 to 15 pounds, while categorical levels simply compare distinct options against one another without implying any order.

Choosing levels also means choosing a baseline. Many experiments deliberately include a zero or standard level, such as no fertilizer at all or the currently used drug dosage, so that every other level can be compared back to a familiar reference point rather than only to each other. Without that baseline level, researchers testing 5 pounds against 10 pounds of fertilizer could conclude that 10 pounds outperforms 5 pounds while never learning whether either amount actually beats using no fertilizer at all.

Together, factor and levels of a factor answer two different design questions: a factor names what is being varied, and its levels specify exactly how it is varied. Every treatment in an experiment, and therefore every group whose results eventually get compared, is defined by picking one level of each factor in the study.
